title: Baby and Newborn Australian Passport Photo Rules
metaTitle: Baby Passport Photo Australia: Newborn and Infant Rules
metaDescription: Australian baby passport photo rules: same size and prints as adults, open mouth allowed under 3, no toys or parent's hands. How to take it.
excerpt: The official rules for a baby, newborn or toddler Australian passport photo, what is relaxed for children under 3, and practical tips for getting the shot.
keyTakeaways: Babies follow the same size and print rules as adults: 2 dye-sublimation prints, 35-40 x 45-50 mm.
Children under 3 may have their mouth open.
No one else can be visible, and no objects such as toys.
The official page does not relax the eyes rule, so aim for open eyes.
intro: **Quick answer:** A baby's Australian passport photo follows the same size and print rules as an adult's: 2 dye-sublimation prints, 35-40 mm wide x 45-50 mm high, with the head 32-36 mm from chin to crown. Children under 3 may have their mouth open. No one else, and no object such as a toy or a parent's hand, can be visible. Aim for open eyes.

> **Important:** The Australian Passport Office recommends a professional passport photo provider and does not recommend online photo services or apps. Use our tool to check or prepare a photo, but always confirm it meets the official guidelines before you apply.
**[Check my photo with the Australian passport photo checker →](/australian-passport-photo-checker)**

sections.heading: What are the rules for a baby passport photo in Australia?

subsections.heading: Same size and print rules as adults
content: There is no special baby size. Your child needs 2 colour photos, 35-40 mm wide x 45-50 mm high, with the head 32-36 mm from chin to crown, taken less than 6 months ago.

They must be dye-sublimation prints on glossy paper of at least 200 gsm, the same as adults. Read the full [Australian passport photo requirements](/guides/australian-passport-photo-requirements) for every rule.

subsections.heading: What is relaxed for children under 3
content: For children under 3, the mouth may be open. You do not need a perfect neutral expression from a baby.
That is the only rule the official page relaxes for this age group.

subsections.heading: What is not relaxed
content: The official page does not say a baby's eyes may be closed, so aim for open eyes. The baby should face the camera straight on, against a plain white or light grey background.
No one else can be visible in the photo, and there should be no objects in the frame.

sections.heading: What is not allowed in a baby passport photo?

subsections.heading: Toys and objects
content: A toy in the photo is one of the official examples of an unacceptable photo. The same goes for dummies, blankets with patterns and anything else in the frame.
Use toys to get your baby's attention from behind the camera, not in the shot.

subsections.heading: A parent's hand or another person
content: A parent's hand in the photo is also listed as unacceptable. No one else can be visible.
If you need to support your baby, keep your hands and arms out of the frame.

subsections.heading: Hats, earbuds and accessories
content: Hats are not allowed, and neither are wireless earbuds. Hearing aids are allowed for babies and children.
Remove headbands and bows that cover the face or the edges of the head.

sections.heading: How do you take a baby passport photo?

subsections.heading: Use a plain white or light grey background
content: The background must be plain white or light grey and contrast with your baby's face.

Tip: lying a young baby on a plain white or light grey sheet, and taking the photo from directly above, can keep the background plain. Make sure the sheet is smooth so there are no shadows from creases.

subsections.heading: Get the baby's face straight on and evenly lit
content: The face must be centred, looking straight at the camera, with the head not tilted. Light should fall evenly with no shadows.
Tip: daylight from a window, facing the baby, usually gives softer light than a camera flash.

subsections.heading: Tips for calm timing and quick photos
content: These are practical tips, not official rules:

- Try after a feed and a nap, when your baby is calm and alert.
- Have a helper make sounds or move a toy just above the camera.
- Take many photos quickly and choose the best one.
- Keep sessions short. Try again later rather than forcing it.

sections.heading: Where can you get a baby's passport photo taken?

subsections.heading: Professional providers who photograph babies
content: The Passport Office recommends a professional provider. Post offices, professional photographers, camera stores, some pharmacies and some chain stores take passport photos.

Ask before you go whether they photograph babies, because some providers are more used to it than others. See [where to get an Australian passport photo](/guides/where-to-get-australian-passport-photo).

subsections.heading: What to ask for
content: Ask for 2 identical colour prints made by dye sublimation on glossy paper of at least 200 gsm, sized for an Australian passport.
Check the head size and that no hands or objects are visible before you leave.

subsections.heading: Why a home photo is risky for babies too
content: The print rules apply to babies as well, and home inkjet prints do not meet them. Babies are also hard to photograph without shadows or a parent's hand in the frame.
A home photo is useful for practice, but use a professional provider for the prints.

sections.heading: How is this different from the UK?

subsections.heading: Australia: open mouth allowed under 3
content: Australia relaxes the mouth rule for children under 3. The official page does not mention closed eyes for babies.

subsections.heading: UK: eyes may be closed under 1
content: In the UK, babies under 1 do not need to have their eyes open. Our [UK child passport photo guide](/uk/uk-child-passport-photo) covers the UK rules.
This is one of several differences between the two countries.

subsections.heading: Why you should not reuse a UK baby photo
content: A UK baby photo may have closed eyes, and the UK allows a smaller head size (29-34 mm) than Australia (32-36 mm). The print rules also differ.
Get a new photo made for the Australian rules.

faq.question: Can my baby's mouth be open in an Australian passport photo?
faq.answer: Yes. For children under 3, the Passport Office allows the mouth to be open. The other rules still apply: plain white or light grey background, face straight on and centred, even lighting, and no other person or object in the photo. Older children need a neutral expression.

faq.question: Can my baby's eyes be closed in an Australian passport photo?
faq.answer: The official Australian guidelines do not say a baby's eyes may be closed, so aim for open eyes. This is different from the UK, where babies under 1 may have closed eyes. Try taking the photo when your baby is calm and alert, such as after a nap.

faq.question: Can I hold my baby in the passport photo?
faq.answer: You can support your baby, but you must not be visible. A parent's hand in the photo is one of the official examples of an unacceptable photo. Lying the baby on a plain sheet, or holding them from behind and out of frame, are common ways to manage this.

faq.question: How old can my baby's passport photo be?
faq.answer: The photo must be less than 6 months old, the same as for adults. Babies change quickly, so a photo taken soon after birth may no longer look like your child by the time you apply. Take a new photo if your baby's appearance has changed a lot.

faq.question: Do babies need two passport photos?
faq.answer: Yes. Babies follow the same rule as adults: 2 colour photos, made by dye sublimation on glossy paper of at least 200 gsm. Ask your provider for 2 identical prints at the Australian size, and check that no hands, toys or other objects appear in them.
